title: PEMF Therapy for Dogs: What to Know
author: Gemma Johnstone
intro:
If your aging or active dog is slowing down or limping, they could be suffering from osteoarthritis or an acute injury. Your dog may initially be prescribed nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), which are the cornerstone of traditional treatment for managing joint stiffness and lameness. However, they aren’t suitable for every dog and can have long-term risks. Fortunately, veterinarians are increasingly adopting multimodal treatment plans that combine medications with rehabilitation therapies to better manage pain and support recovery.

In This Article

Pulsed electromagnetic field therapy (PEMF) is a non-invasive wound healing and pain management technology that’s growing in popularity in human and veterinary medicine. Read on to learn whether PEMF therapy for dogs is a treatment option worth discussing with your veterinarian.
full_content:
{'What Is PEMF Therapy and How Does It Work?': 'PEMF therapy uses electromagnetic waves to carry energy that stimulates biological activity within tissues. The treatment is delivered via a device that emits signals targeted to a specific part of the body.

Dr. Christine Jurek is the Medical Director at Thrive Pet Healthcare partner TOPS Veterinary Rehabilitation in Grayslake, Illinois. She explains that light or sound waves experience some interference when the body’s tissue absorbs them. However, electromagnetic waves penetrate deeply with minimal resistance, allowing the signal to reach structures such as muscles, joints, and bones.

PEMF therapy is believed to influence cellular processes involved in healing and inflammation. “It actually changes the cell membranes and makes them more permeable, and ultimately it increases a substance called nitric oxide, which is a key substance that increases blood flow and reduces inflammation,” Dr. Jurek says.

Improved circulation helps deliver oxygen and nutrients to damaged tissues and may support healing. There’s even research suggesting that PEMF therapy stimulates the release of endorphins and serotonin, chemicals associated with pain regulation and mood.

', 'When Is PEMF Therapy Used for Dogs?': 'Dr. Jurek explains that she most often uses PEMF therapy for managing pain and inflammation associated with canine osteoarthritis. This progressive joint disease is common in dogs and leads to chronic pain, stiffness, and decreased mobility. PEMF therapy may help reduce discomfort and improve mobility for some dogs.

Veterinary providers can also use PEMF therapy to support the healing in a range of other conditions, including:

Some owners of canine athletes and working dogs use PEMF therapy to promote tissue health and minimize the risk of injury. Early research has even explored its potential to help reduce stress levels in dogs with separation anxiety.

The FDA has also approved PEMF therapy for various conditions in humans, including urinary incontinence, depression, anxiety, and certain cancers. However, further research is necessary in these areas of veterinary medicine.

', 'How Effective Is PEMF Therapy for Dogs?': 'PEMF therapy has a strong safety profile, and the promising early research means it’s increasingly viewed as a useful adjunct or standalone therapy, particularly for chronic musculoskeletal problems.

Some studies in dogs with osteoarthritis have shown improvements clinical signs such in pain and mobility following repeated PEMF treatments. Other research has evidenced reductions in inflammatory markers and postoperative pain following spinal surgery.

However, veterinary research is still developing. “The studies that we have are fairly well written, and results are promising, but there are not enough of them,” Dr. Jurek says. “Just like every other newly developed technology, we have a lot to learn. However, we’ve got enough information to determine that this is an overall safe treatment, and we’ve got reasonable evidence that it’s effective.”

It’s also important to recognize that treatment results may vary depending on the device used, the frequency and intensity of the electromagnetic signal, and the treatment schedule.

', 'What Are the Risks, Limitations, and Side Effects?': 'One reason PEMF therapy is popular in veterinary rehabilitation is its strong safety profile. It’s non‑invasive, does not generate heat, and is generally well tolerated by dogs. To date, significant adverse effects have not been documented when PEMF therapy is used appropriately.

However, there are situations where veterinarians exercise caution, specifically in pregnant dogs, dogs with tumors, and dogs who are prone to seizures.

“We tend not to use them in pregnant patients, because we don’t know what effect the cell signaling might have on the fetus,” Dr. Jurek says.\xa0Early research suggests that certain electromagnetic signals may suppress tumor growth, which is why researchers are exploring PEMF therapy as a potential cancer treatment. However, until more research is available, most veterinarians avoid using it on tumors. Use in dog with seizures must also be done cautiously because there may be potential to trigger seizure activity.

Another limitation is that PEMF therapy requires an accurate diagnosis and correct targeting of the treatment area. Using an at-home device without identifying the underlying cause of pain or applying it to the wrong location could delay the right type of medical care.

“Having that partnership with a medical professional is critical to the success of the treatment, as well as to eliminate some pitfalls in potentially misusing the device,” Dr. Jurek emphasizes.

', 'How Is PEMF Therapy Administered?': 'PEMF therapy can be provided in veterinary clinics or at home using portable devices. Sessions typically last between 10 and 60 minutes, depending on the condition and equipment used. While some dogs show temporary improvement after a single session, benefits are usually cumulative and develop with repeated treatments over days or weeks.

“The at-home devices are small and portable, and the pet either lies on top of a mat with magnets embedded within it, or they have portable loop devices that you can put on a specific area,” Dr. Jurek says.

', 'At Home PEMF Therapy vs. In-Office Treatments': 'The advantage of attending a veterinary rehabilitation clinic is that many of them incorporate PEMF therapy as part of a broader treatment plan. It means you can be sure the treatment is targeting the right area, and your veterinarian can tweak treatment based on your dog’s response.

At-home devices have become increasingly popular because they allow dogs to receive more frequent treatments without repeated clinic visits. The upfront cost of a device typically ranges from about $300 to $2,000, which can be less expensive than the cost of ongoing appointments over time.

However, Dr. Jurek warns that not all devices are supported by solid research. “There’s a lot of devices on the market, and unfortunately, they’re not all vetted, and they can make all sorts of label claims, but they might not be true,” she says.

Different devices produce different electromagnetic intensities and pulse frequencies, so their effects may not be interchangeable. Some are designed to treat a specific part of the body, while others provide whole-body exposure.

Working closely with your veterinary rehabilitation practitioner ensures you can select a device that’s appropriate for your dog’s condition.

', 'When Is It Worth Considering PEMF Therapy for Dogs?': 'PEMF therapy isn’t a cure-all, and research is still evolving. However, if you’re looking for ways to help your dog manage pain or recover from an injury or surgery more quickly, it could be one tool worth discussing with a veterinarian or veterinary rehabilitation specialist.

While PEMF therapy can sometimes be used as a standalone treatment, it’s most often part of a multimodal treatment plan for chronic conditions such as osteoarthritis or slow-healing injuries. Veterinarians may combine it with medications, therapeutic exercise, weight management, laser therapy, and other rehabilitation techniques.

Dr. Jurek stresses the importance of strengthening and stability exercises alongside pain management in conditions like osteoarthritis. “If we don’t strengthen the tissues around the joint, if we don’t make the muscles stronger, that joint will continue to deteriorate,” she says.

title: Swollen Lymph Nodes in Dogs: Everything You Need to Know
author: Gemma Johnstone
intro:
If you’re petting your dog in that favorite spot under their chin and you feel a new lump, it’s not something to ignore. Depending on its position, it could be a swollen lymph node. Swollen lymph nodes in dogs aren’t always life-threatening, but they’re definitely worth bringing up to your vet.

In This Article

Lymph nodes are a vital part of the immune system, and when they’re enlarged, it can be a sign that the body is responding to something unusual. Causes range from minor infections to more serious diseases like cancer. Knowing what to look for means you can get prompt veterinary attention and potentially an early diagnosis. Catching something early could save your dog’s life.
full_content:
{'What Are Lymph Nodes in Dogs?': 'Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped glands that are an important interconnected part of the immune system. They contain lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell, that help fight infection and illness.

Kate Vickery, VMD, MS, DACVIM (Oncology), CVA, is an Associate Clinical Professor of Medical Oncology at the Flint Animal Cancer Center at Colorado State University. She describes lymph nodes as being like the body’s waste depot. They filter lymph fluid, which carries proteins, fats, waste products, and immune cells throughout the body.

“If a dog has any inflammation in a specific area of the body, the lymph node will be activated, and that will call in the immune system to help address the inflammation or infection,” she explains.

When the immune system is activated, lymph nodes can enlarge significantly as they fill with immune cells or, in some cases, abnormal cells.

It’s also sometimes possible to detect those in the armpits (axillary) and in the groin area (inguinal). There are also lymph nodes inside the chest and abdominal cavities.

', 'How to Tell if Your Dog’s Lymph Nodes in Dogs Are Swollen?': 'When your dog is healthy, lymph nodes are small and difficult to detect by touch. In small dogs, they’re often around the size of a pea, and in larger breeds, they can be grape-sized.

Even if the lymph nodes are slightly enlarged, it can be hard to distinguish them from the surrounding tissue. However, some swollen lymph nodes can grow to be up to 10 times their normal size, becoming hard to miss very quickly.

“I recommend that owners have an understanding of where on the body to feel for the lymph nodes and to get a sense for what their dog’s ‘normal’ feels like,” Dr. Vickery says. “This way, they will have a better understanding of when things become abnormal.” She describes abnormal lymph nodes as feeling “like a whole walnut in the shell underneath the skin, where it’s firm to the touch.”

Some enlarged nodes can be painful to the touch, especially when caused by infections. Others may not cause your dog any discomfort.

', 'What Causes Swollen Lymph Nodes in Dogs?': 'There are various causes of swollen lymph nodes in dogs, but the most common include infection, inflammation, and cancer.

When the body detects invading infections, it produces more white blood cells, which collect in nearby lymph nodes.

According to Dr. Vickery, bacterial or fungal infections may cause swollen lymph nodes across the body, but more commonly, the swelling is localized to the nodes near the infection site. Skin wounds, ear infections, and upper respiratory infections are all common causes of localized swelling.

Vector-borne diseases such as Lyme disease or ehrlichiosis from ticks, leishmaniasis, or tularemia may also lead to widespread lymph node enlargement.

Inflammation can also cause lymph nodes to swell. “[This can include] reactive lymph node enlargement due to focal inflammation,” Dr. Vickery explains. “Dental disease is a good example of this, especially in older dogs.” She also lists cutaneous lupus erythematosus (an autoimmune skin condition) and sterile granulomatous lymphadenitis (often called puppy strangles or juvenile cellulitis) as culprits.

Allergies to environmental triggers or food can also lead to inflammation throughout the body, temporarily enlarging lymph nodes.

Lymphoma, a cancer of the lymphatic system, is the most common cancer associated with swollen lymph nodes in dogs. According to Dr. Vickery, you often see the ones at the back of the knees, under the jaw, and in front of the shoulder enlarged.

“Cancer can also spread (metastasize) to a lymph node,” Dr. Vickery says. “For example, a dog with an oral tumor may have cancer spread to one or both of the mandibular lymph nodes, which causes just those lymph nodes to be enlarged.”

', 'Other Signs for Dogs With Swollen Lymph Nodes': 'In some cases, your dog may not have any other noticeable signs besides swollen lymph nodes. However, Dr. Vickery says swelling and edema (accumulation of fluid) in the tissues around the lymph node are possible, and the swelling may be painful to the touch.

If you notice any swelling or other concerning changes, don’t delay in contacting your veterinarian. Early evaluation and treatment can lead to a better outcome for your dog.

', 'Diagnosis of Swollen Lymph Nodes in Dogs': 'Your veterinarian will begin by conducting a thorough physical exam and discussing your dog’s history and symptoms with you.

The most common diagnostic test for enlarged lymph nodes is a fine-needle aspiration. This involves your veterinarian inserting a small needle into the lymph node to collect cells for examination under a microscope. This testing can help determine whether the swelling relates to infection, inflammation, or cancer.

According to Dr. Vickery, additional tests may include:

', 'Treatment of Swollen Lymph Nodes in Dogs': 'Treatment varies widely depending on the underlying cause and its severity.

When your dog has an infection, your veterinarian may prescribe antibiotics, antifungal medication, or a dental procedure. Anti-inflammatory medications, such as corticosteroids, may help treat inflammatory or allergic conditions. Some dogs with severe infections may require supportive treatment in a veterinary hospital to help them recover.

If your dog receives a lymphoma diagnosis, chemotherapy is the main treatment. Dr. Vickery acknowledges that, while this may sound scary, veterinary chemotherapy is usually tolerated well by dogs. It uses lower doses than the human version, designed to slow the disease’s progression while preserving quality of life. “Some of our canine patients may experience a little bit of a picky appetite or loose stool while they’re going through treatment, but it’s usually very manageable,” Dr. Vickery explains.

While chemo can help to put lymphoma into remission for a period of time, it won’t be the right treatment or accessible in every situation. Veterinarians often prescribe anti-inflammatory steroids as part of a palliative care treatment plan.

', 'Prognosis for Dogs With Swollen Lymph Nodes': 'Dogs with infections or inflammatory conditions generally make a full recovery once the underlying problem is treated. You can expect your dog’s lymph nodes to return to their normal size within a few weeks.

Lymphoma in dogs isn’t a curable disease. With chemotherapy treatment, the median survival is about one year, although Dr. Vickery notes that she has had some patients live a good quality of life for several years. Without treatment, lymphoma typically progresses quickly. However, with appropriate palliative treatment, many dog owners are still be able to enjoy a comfortable few weeks or months with their dog.

title: Concussions in Dogs: Signs, Symptoms, Treatments
author: Nandini Maharaj
intro:
We often think of concussions as happening to people while they’re working or playing competitive sports. But pets are also at risk of brain injury. Concussion in dogs is “a very serious medical problem that can become life-threatening,” says Dr. Dottie Hagler, DVM, DACVIM, board-certified veterinary neurologist and medical director at Pet Specialists of Austin. “The good news is that dogs are incredibly resilient, and many patients who suffer from this condition actually go on to survive and have a great quality of life, but early intervention is key.”

In This Article

If you suspect your dog has a concussion, seek veterinary care right away. If you suspect your dog has a concussion, seek veterinary care immediately to improve their chances of recovery and prevent complications. We asked veterinarians about the symptoms, causes, and treatment of concussion in dogs canine concussions.

{'What Is a Concussion in Dogs?': 'A concussion occurs “when the brain hits the skull and undergoes trauma,” says Dr. Veronica Villanueva, DVM, medical director at VEG Anaheim Hills. “A more severe concussion is when they get backlash, where the brain hits the front and back of the skull.” This kind of trauma can cause brain swelling and even seizures.

“In veterinary medicine, we refer to concussions as a traumatic brain injury or TBI,” Dr. Hagler says. “Statistically, about one out of every four dogs who have some type of blunt trauma to their head will have a significant traumatic brain injury.” Such injuries may include a skull fracture or a fracture that causes compression of the brain, and there may be pieces of skull in the brain.

“We can also see intracranial bleeding, and that can put additional pressure on or inside of the brain, and contusive injury where the brain comes in contact with the side of the skull during the trauma,” Dr. Hagler says. Dogs may also have polytrauma, meaning they have additional injuries to their body. “They may have been in some type of vehicular accident, or been dropped on their heads, or have had a heavy object fall on their heads,” she explains.

In less severe cases, concussions generally involve a functional disturbance rather thanas opposed to structural damage. With a functional disturbance, “a CT scan or an MRI would be completely normal, and the dogs would make a full recovery with rest and monitoring,” says Dr. Eliza O’Callaghan, DVM, managing veterinarian for Small Door Veterinary. She explains that a functional disturbance is a temporary neurologic disturbance, such as dizziness, that affects the dog’s functioning. In contrast, structural damage refers to a bruise or a bleed.

', 'Symptoms of Canine Concussions': 'The most common symptom of concussion in dogs is diminished or dull mentation, meaning their level of awareness, Dr. Hagler says. They may be unable to walk or have difficulty maintaining their balance. “Patients can come in even worse than that, where they’re in a coma or having seizures,” she adds.

In a petit mal seizure, dogs may roll into a tight ball, stiff and shaking, Dr. Villanueva says. Other signs are a head tremor or seeming disoriented. In Conversely, dogs can have a grand mal seizure, dogs may flail their legs, vocalize, urinate, or defecate themselves,” she says.

The onset of symptoms tends to occur immediately following the trauma. “An exception would be patients who have an intracranial bleed that’s slow,” Dr. Hagler says. “In a patient like that, it may take a few hours for them to become symptomatic.”

Physical and behavioral symptoms of canine concussion include:

“The symptoms we see are indicative of where in the brain the problem is,” Dr. Hagler says. Some parts of the brain require more nutrients than others, making them more susceptible to metabolic injuries, such as a disruption in nutrient processing or energy production. For example, an injury to the front of the brain is more likely to cause behavioral or personality changes.

Another example is an injury to the brain stem, which controls breathing. “Injuring that part of the brain is going to carry a much more guarded prognosis,” Dr. Hagler says. Fortunately, these injuries are less common because the brain stem is tucked away at the back of the brain. “When patients are exhibiting symptoms of a brain stem injury, often, it’s because the front of the brain has been injured and becomes swollen, causing pressure on the back of the brain,” she explains.

', 'Causes of Concussion in Dogs': 'One of the most common causes of TBI in dogs is getting hit by a car, but it’s not the only one. “I’ve also had very small patients who jumped out of their owner’s arms and fell on their heads,” Dr. Hagler says. They can also have a heavy object fall on their head. “Some of these patients are so small that it really doesn’t take much to cause a serious brain injury,” she says.

Dogs can also suffer falls from grooming tables and furniture. Another cause of brain injury is “really rough play, where two dogs have a collision, causing a minor concussion,” Dr. O’Callaghan says. Such injuries can also happen in working dogs, hunting dogs, and dogs who participate in sports such as agility. “They’re at a higher risk of exposure to high-impact environments and physical exertion,” Dr. Villanueva says.

Aside from blunt force trauma, Dr. O’Callaghan explains that sudden acceleration or deceleration of the head or neck, like in a car accident, can also cause concussions. This motion can cause the brain to collide with the inside of the skull, causing an injury. Dr. Villanueva agrees, adding that dogs can get whiplash and develop a concussion.

“We take our pets everywhere now, which is wonderful, but they don’t have a seatbelt,” she says. She sees this a lot with\xa0 small breed dogs. They can fly and hit the windshield and have permanent head trauma. In addition, small breed dogs like the Chihuahua and Pomeranian have what’s called an open fontanelle or a soft spot in the skull, which can put them at risk of a brain injury.

', 'Immediate Actions and Emergency Care for Head Trauma': 'If you observe any type of head trauma, especially a car accident or high-speed collision, Dr. Hagler recommends taking your dog to the nearest veterinarian immediately. Even if they don’t show initial problems, dogs should be evaluated by a veterinarian. “Dogs are very good at hiding their injuries,” she says. “Often, patients have to be in a lot of pain before they start screaming or crying.”

A veterinarian can provide initial stabilization, often with medications that reduce pressure and swelling. Treatment typically also includes:

“The initial neurologic presentation of the patients is just as important as the trend we observe over time,” adds Dr. Hagler. Veterinarians use a grading system called the modified Glasgow Coma Scale, or small animal coma scale, to assess whether a patient is getting better or worsening. These scales provide an objective assessment of the patient’s condition and are helpful in intensive care unit settings where multiple veterinarians treat patients.

“Often, in these patients, we also need some form of advanced imaging like a CAT scan or MRI,” Dr. Hagler says. These tests help determine whether patients need additional intervention, such as decompressive brain surgery. They may also need another procedure to stabilize injuries sustained during the initial accident.

', 'Diagnosing Canine Concussion': 'Not all incidents occur on our watch. Dogs could be playing outside when an injury happens, or you may be out of the house when they slip and fall or run into a wall. If you notice any neurological symptoms, such as disorientation or a loss of coordination, Dr. Villanueva recommends taking your dog to a veterinarian right away for early assessment and treatment.

“You need to be vigilant within the first 24 to 48 hours following a head trauma because there can be life-threatening complications like brain bleeding or swelling, and they can develop very slowly,” she says. “A veterinarian can perform a neurologic exam to see if there are deficits that the owner may not be able to see.” Even if your dog seems okay, if you suspect they’ve had head trauma, bring them to see a veterinarian. Dogs can’t tell us what’s wrong, and symptoms aren’t always immediately visible.

In diagnosing concussions in dogs, the veterinarian will perform a full physical examination from nose to tail. They will take your dog’s history and perform a neurologic examination. “We’re going to watch them walk and see if they’re having any ataxia,” Dr. Villanueva says. “We’re also going to flip their paws upside down because the natural response is to correct it and put their foot the right way.”

The latter is called conscious proprioception, which is “a way of testing whether the dog knows where their feet are in space,” Dr. O’Callaghan explains. Other assessment tools include taking your dog’s blood pressure, having them balance on one leg, and checking their reflexes. For example, a dog should blink when you put your finger up to their eyes.

If the trauma is mild or the injury seems minor, “at minimum, we would want a pet parent to keep their dog with them for observation, for the rest of that day to make sure they didn’t take a turn for the worse,” Dr. Hagler says.

', 'Treatment and Recovery from Canine Concussion': 'Treatment and prognosis depend on the location and severity of the dog’s injury, and the type of stabilization needed. “The real cornerstone of treatment is strict rest and observation and making sure they don’t deteriorate from the state they’re in,” Dr. O’Callaghan says. Crate rest is ideal, but you can have your dog confined to a small room or area where there’s no furniture or steps for them to climb and injure themselves further.

AKC is a participant in affiliate advertising programs designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees by advertising and linking to akc.org. If you purchase a product through this article, we may receive a portion of the sale.

Out of an abundance of caution, a veterinarian may recommend hospitalization for initial monitoring. Among patients requiring hospitalization, “some dogs improve very rapidly and are discharged in 24 or 48 hours,” Dr. Hagler says. Other patients require a longer hospitalization. For example, a patient who undergoes a decompressive brain surgery may need to stay in the hospital for a longer period than one with a less severe injury.

“If we see a neurologic deficit, we’re going to treat and would hospitalize them, because we want to prevent permanent damage,” Dr. Villanueva says. “The sooner we can start, the better.” Permanent damage can result from brain pressure or bleeding. For example, if the brain hits the front and back of the skull, this can result in a severe injury. “There’s a French term for it called contrecoup brain injury,” Dr. Villanueva says. In addition, the veterinarian will monitor the dog’s vital signs, including their blood pressure.

“If we’re seeing neurologic signs, we’re probably going to give them an opioid such as hydromorphone or gabapentin for neuropathic pain,” Dr. Villanueva says. A vet may also prescribe diuretics like mannitol to help reduce brain swelling and anti-seizure medications to treat seizures.

“If your dog is in pain, please don’t give any human medications to them,” she says, adding that “Tylenol and Ibuprofen are toxic to dogs.” In cases where the vet doesn’t observe neurologic symptoms, but the dog is experiencing pain, they may suggest treating the dog on an outpatient basis.

If the amount of brain trauma is severe, a veterinary neurologist can request an MRI or CT scan to assess the brain further and detect any bleeding or swelling, Dr. Villanueva says. “If there’s any form of brain trauma or thoughts of a concussion, we would recommend doing an MRI or CT scan right away,” she says. Knowing the severity of the injury will help determine the prognosis.

“In general, once a patient starts improving, the prognosis tends to be good,” Dr. Hagler says. Many patients go on to have a good quality of life. That said, “it’s not uncommon for dogs who have survived severe head injury to have some type of permanent neurologic deficit, like difficulty seeing out of one eye, having seizures, or walking with an uncoordinated gait,” she says.

As your dog is recovering, you can take them outside on a short leash for toileting. All three experts agree that you should use a harness instead of a collar to avoid pulling on their head or neck. Dogs generally recover from a concussion within 24 to 72 hours. Dr. O’Callaghan recommends a week of rest to be on the safe side. Once neurologic signs resolve, dogs can gradually return to normal activity.

Dr. Villanueva stresses the importance of not overexerting your dog as they’re recovering. Avoid taking them to the park or allowing them to run around. “Just keep them calm and have them rest,” she says. Although infrequent, some patients may require physical rehabilitation. Full rehabilitation, whenever possible, may take a long time, Dr. Hagler says.

', 'The Importance of Prevention and Early Intervention': 'There are several things you can do to prevent TBI in dogs or reduce the risk of permanent damage. “One of the most important things is to invest in some type of restraint device for inside a vehicle,” Dr. Hagler says. A patient of hers, who was in a car accident, wasn’t restrained and developed a compressive skull fracture that required surgery. Despite having a good quality of life, this patient developed seizures.

Dr. Villanueva has seen similar accidents in her practice. She recommends not allowing your dog to sit in the back of your truck. Your dog could get excited and jump out of the vehicle or get injured if you slam on the brakes.

Another way to prevent concussions is to take precautions at home and outdoors. Indoors, remove any heavy furniture or objects your dog might run into, Dr. Villanueva says. When you’re outdoors, keep your dog on a leash or in a fenced-in area. With working dogs, make sure you’re in an open area with no trees or obstructions in their path.

title: Laryngeal Paralysis in Dogs: Causes, Signs, and Treatment
author: Gemma Johnstone
intro:
Have you noticed your older dog slowing down when out on walks, panting more than usual, or making strange breathing sounds? It could be more than just age catching up with them. Laryngeal paralysis is a progressive condition that affects a dog’s ability to breathe normally, and, in severe cases, it can be life-threatening.

In This Article

Because this condition often develops slowly, the early signs can be easy to overlook. While there’s no cure for laryngeal paralysis in dogs, securing a timely diagnosis and taking proactive management steps can help keep your pet comfortable and enjoying a good quality of life for longer.
full_content:
{'What Is Laryngeal Paralysis in Dogs?': 'The larynx, or voice box, sits at the top of the trachea (windpipe). It allows air to enter the lungs and prevents food and liquids from going into the airway when swallowing.

Small muscles in the larynx pull what’s called the arytenoid cartilages. In healthy dogs, these open in the larynx open during breathing. They widen the airway so air can move through freely. The larynx relaxes again when the dog exhales. In dogs with laryngeal paralysis (sometimes shortened to “lar-par”), the nerves controlling these muscles don’t work properly.

“When these muscles fail, the cartilages remain in a relaxed position, obstructing the opening into the trachea,” Michael Tillson, DVM, MS, DACVS, the Bruce Pratt Eminent Scholar Chair in Small Animal Surgery at Auburn University College of Veterinary Medicine, explains. “This obstruction, and the associated struggle to breathe, increases when a dog needs to increase their respiration (such as during activities, when excited, or when panting due to hot weather).”

', 'What Causes Laryngeal Paralysis in Dogs?': 'Laryngeal paralysis in dogs is a complex condition that can be congenital (present at birth) or acquired later in life.

AKC is a participant in affiliate advertising programs designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees by advertising and linking to akc.org. If you purchase a product through this article, we may receive a portion of the sale.

Inherited forms of lar-par, which tends to appear in dogs under 1one year old, is not common. However, breeds including the Bouvier des Flandres, Black Russian Terrier, Bulldog, Dalmatian, Leonberger, Rottweiler, and Siberian Husky have been reported to have inherited forms or lar-par.

Laryngeal paralysis is much more common in older dogs, especially in large and giant breeds. It’s also more commonly seen in male dogs than in females. Labrador Retrievers are one of the most frequently affected, but it’s also seen in Golden Retrievers, Irish Setters, Saint Bernards, and Great Danes.

In many senior dogs, there is no identifiable underlying cause, and the laryngeal paralysis is referred to as “idiopathic.” However, lar-par is often attributed to a broader generalized degenerative nerve disorder that affects multiple areas of the body. In these cases, it’s referred to as geriatric-onset laryngeal paralysis-polyneuropathy (GOLP-P), which can also affect the esophagus.

Other less common causes of\xa0acquired\xa0laryngeal paralysis in dogs include neck trauma, surgical injury, tumors, or endocrine disorders such as\xa0hypothyroidism.\xa0

', 'Signs & Symptoms of Laryngeal Paralysis in Dogs': 'Early signs of laryngeal paralysis in dogs can vary and are often subtle and slow to develop. As a result, owners may attribute a dog’s initial symptoms to the natural aging process. However, often the “slowing down” they see is because their dogs have reduced stamina due to an impaired ability to breathe properly.

Some common subtle early signs include:

As the condition worsens, which can take months or years, your dog may show\xa0additional\xa0signs, including:\xa0

AKC is a participant in affiliate advertising programs designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees by advertising and linking to akc.org. If you purchase a product through this article, we may receive a portion of the sale.

Heat intolerance is a particularly important red flag. “A critical factor in understanding laryngeal paralysis is that affected dogs have limited ability to effectively increase their respiration rate,” Dr. Tillson explains. “This can seriously compromise their ability to dissipate heat from their bodies through panting.” Even mild exertion or warm weather can trigger respiratory distress and heatstroke.

If your dog shows severe breathing difficulties, has blue or purple-tinged gums, or suddenly collapses, seek veterinary attention immediately. Respiratory distress is a medical emergency, and quick action can be life-saving.

', 'How is Laryngeal Paralysis Diagnosed?': 'The definitive diagnostic test for laryngeal paralysis in dogs is to examine the larynx under light anesthesia. Once your dog is sedated, your veterinarian can safely observe the movement of the arytenoid cartilages as your dog breathes.

“The [dog]’s history and physical examination, as well as other imaging tests (including thoracic films, ultrasound, and CT imaging) can be useful in heightening the suspicion of lar-par or in providing supportive evidence,” Dr. Tillson notes. “However, few veterinary surgeons would undertake surgical intervention without the visual confirmation.”

In some cases, your veterinarian may also order\xa0additional\xa0tests, such as blood work or a neurologic exam, to help\xa0identify\xa0suspected underlying causes.\xa0

', 'Treatment of Laryngeal Paralysis in Dogs': 'Currently, there isn’t a cure for laryngeal paralysis in dogs, so treatment focuses on managing symptoms and preventing life-threatening breathing problems.

AKC is a participant in affiliate advertising programs designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees by advertising and linking to akc.org. If you purchase a product through this article, we may receive a portion of the sale.

Veterinarians can often handle mild cases of laryngeal paralysis in dogs with conservative intervention. “Medical management strategies include altering the pet’s lifestyle to prevent respiratory crises,” Dr. Tillson explains.

Management and treatment options may include:

AKC is a participant in affiliate advertising programs designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees by advertising and linking to akc.org. If you purchase a product through this article, we may receive a portion of the sale.

If your dog has a serious breathing crisis requiring emergency care, your veterinarian may administer oxygen therapy, intravenous fluids, sedation, and cooling measures. In severe cases, temporary intubation (a procedure in which a tube is inserted into the trachea to\xa0maintain\xa0an open airway) may be necessary to\xa0assist in\xa0breathing.

While medical management techniques can help some dogs temporarily, they don’t correct the airway obstruction. Surgery can’t fully restore laryngeal function, but it can often significantly improve breathing and quality of life.

The most widely performed surgery for laryngeal paralysis is unilateral arytenoid lateralization, which is commonly called a “tie-back.”

“It allows the surgeon to permanently abduct one of the laryngeal cartilages by pulling it to the side and locking it in place using permanent suture material,” Dr. Tillson explains. “This opens half of the airway, permitting an easier passage of air during inhalation.”

Most dogs tolerate the procedure well, especially when performed by an experienced veterinary surgeon.

“A successful ‘tie-back’ should dramatically reduce the potential for a respiratory crisis and typically allows the dog to resume routine, if somewhat limited, activities,” Dr. Tillson explains.

As with any surgery, there are risks. The most common serious complication is\xa0aspiration\xa0pneumonia, which occurs when food, water, or stomach contents enter the lungs. According to Dr. Tillson, this\xa0typically\xa0occurs in the immediate post-operative period.

AKC is a participant in affiliate advertising programs designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees by advertising and linking to akc.org. If you purchase a product through this article, we may receive a portion of the sale.

After surgery, you should avoid letting your dog swim and feed small meals to reduce the risk of aspiration pneumonia. You will also need to monitor closely for signs such as coughing, fever, lethargy, nasal discharge, or loss of appetite.

“There are various other surgical procedures available to be used by some veterinary surgeons,” Dr. Tillson says. “I find these are the most useful if the ‘tie-back’ procedure fails or is inappropriate for another reason.” He explains that future treatments include laryngeal stents to keep the laryngeal cartilages apart.

', 'Prognosis for Laryngeal Paralysis in Dogs': '“It’s important to realize GOLP-P is thought to be a progressive condition, but we are not clear on how quickly any individual dog will progress,” Dr. Tillson explains. Some dogs can remain stable with mild signs for years, while others decline into respiratory distress much more rapidly.

Many dogs live comfortably for months or years after diagnosis with proper medical management. Successful surgery can also result in dramatic improvement for some dogs, with many\xa0often regaining\xa0stamina and energy after having serious breathing difficulties.

By recognizing the signs early and communicating with your primary care veterinarian and, when\xa0appropriate, a board-certified surgeon, you can help ensure the best possible outcome for your dog.

'}

title: Supporting Your Dog’s Mobility, Joints, Skin, and Coat Through Every Life Stage
author: Balchem
intro:

Dogs change as they grow up, and their nutritional needs change as well. From puppies to senior dogs, maintaining healthy mobility, joint function, and skin and coat quality are essential to your dog’s quality of life. Focusing on proper nutrition at each life stage can help your dog stay active and feeling their best for years to come.
full_content:
{'Starting Strong\xa0With\xa0Proper Nutrition as Puppies': 'When dogs are young, everything in their body is still being built. Their bones, joints, muscles, skin, and even their immune defenses are still developing. What they eat during their puppy years\xa0doesn’t\xa0just fuel growth for that day. Their diet helps\xa0determine\xa0how their body will hold up years down the road.\xa0

Early nutrition plays\xa0a\xa0important role in normal joint development, strong connective tissues, and a healthy skin barrier. Supporting these systems as early as possible helps set the foundation for lifelong health.\xa0

All puppies need high-quality nutrition. But some puppies, like large and giant\xa0breeds\xa0might need extra care. Dogs who plan to compete in dog sports may also need special consideration for their diets.\xa0

', 'Supporting Your Dogs’ Health as They Age': 'As dogs mature, daily wear and\xa0tear\xa0on joints\xa0increases. This is especially true for sporting,\xa0large‑breed, or working dogs.\xa0

Many\xa0say\xa0“a dog’s coat is a portal to the health of the inside”.\xa0Skin and coat health can fluctuate due to seasonal shedding, allergens, or stress. Skin is the body’s largest organ and the first line of defense against the outside world. Good nutrition helps develop a strong skin barrier, which supports immunity protection and resilience to environmental stressors later in life. As dogs age, their physiological systems become more fragile.\xa0

Dogs are more prone to joint stiffness, reduced mobility, thinner skin, and duller coats as they age. Targeted support through nutrition can help keep them comfortable, flexible, and looking healthy as their bodies slow down.\xa0

', 'Supporting Your Senior Dog’s Health': 'As dogs age,\xa0it’s\xa0common to think they may slow down. And in many ways, they might. But this\xa0doesn’t\xa0always have to be the case. Things like helping your dog\xa0maintain\xa0a healthy weight, and keeping their muscles strong can go a long way. Many senior dogs can still live\xa0a very active, healthy lifestyle even as they age.\xa0

Many conformation events, for example, will have specific classes for Veterans. This class is\xa0designated\xa0for senior dogs, and most still have\xa0mobility\xa0of the champions they truly are.\xa0

If you suspect your senior dog may be having mobility issues, there are signs you can look out for. Initial signs of mobility issues include slower overall movement, visible changes in your dog’s gait, reluctance to jump on or\xa0off of\xa0the couch, or take stairs. .\xa0You may also notice stiffness or difficulty standing up after rest, and less interest in taking their normal walks.\xa0\xa0Once this is noticeable, talk to your veterinarian about\xa0next\xa0steps.\xa0

', 'Skin & Coat Support Nutrients That Go Beyond Appearance': 'Healthy skin and a shiny coat are more than cosmetic. A healthy coat is a visible sign of overall wellness. Several critical nutrients play an important role in maintaining skin barrier, coat quality, and the tissues that support comfortable movement.\xa0

When skin and coat are well supported, it often reflects balanced nutrition. Minerals and vitamins help the body absorb and use these vital nutrients effectively.\xa0That’s\xa0why many veterinarians and pet nutritionists recommend combination formulas rather than\xa0single‑ingredient\xa0supplements.\xa0\xa0No matter which combination of ingredients you choose, make sure to find high quality ingredients from brands you trust.\xa0

By supporting your dog nutritionally before problems arise, you can help them stay active, comfortable, and confident at\xa0every life\xa0stage. When your dog feels good on the inside, it\xa0shows\xa0on the outside.\xa0

', 'How Supplements Can Help Support Your Dog’s Joint Health': 'One\xa0option\xa0to help your senior\xa0dog’s\xa0joints is through joint supplements. Many modern pet supplements combine ingredients that each play a slightly different role,\xa0kind of like\xa0a maintenance team that keeps everything moving smoothly.\xa0

Think of glucosamine as a building block for joints. It helps support cartilage—the smooth, material that cushions joints and allows bones to glide without grinding. Over time, normal activity causes wear and tear, and glucosamine helps the body\xa0maintain\xa0that\xa0cushioning\xa0so movement stays smooth,\xa0flexible\xa0and comfortable.\xa0

Chondroitin works\xa0hand‑in‑hand\xa0with glucosamine. Its\xa0main role\xa0is helping joints hold onto water within the joint. This keeps cartilage flexible and resilient, rather than dry and brittle.\xa0It’s\xa0like keeping a sponge moist, so it stays springy instead of cracking.\xa0

Methylsulfonylmethane\xa0(MSM) supplies\xa0what’s\xa0known as “bioavailable sulfur.” This is an essential mineral that the body uses to build connective tissues like cartilage, tendons, ligaments. MSM supports joint comfort and helps\xa0maintain\xa0a normal inflammatory balance that allows dogs to stay active without too much stiffness. When found in the body, MSM provides a natural source of bioavailable sulfur. Bioavailable sulfur is essential to building collagen and\xa0maintain\xa0their strength and flexibility. Collagen is found in cartilage, tendons, ligaments, skin, and connective tissues, which hold everything together. By supporting collagen integrity, MSM helps joints stay strong and flexible while also contributing to healthy skin elasticity and a strong coat. MSM also supports keratin structure, keeping your dog’s coat looking and feeling healthy.\xa0

Omega‑3 Fatty Acids (O3FA; EPA & DHA) are found in fish oil and algae oil. These unique omega‑3 fatty acids modulate normal anti-inflammatory responses throughout the body. Adequate omega‑3 intake helps\xa0maintain\xa0soft, hydrated skin and a glossy coat, while also helping to reduce dander. Sources of O3FA are important for skin and coat health. Green-lipped mussels\xa0contain\xa0omega-3 fatty acids, as well as glycosaminoglycans and natural antioxidants. Together, these compounds help support joint function, comfortable mobility, and overall movement—especially in active or aging dogs.\xa0

In many joint supplements that support total-body health, you might find ingredients like zinc and biotin. Zinc is an essential trace mineral that supports skin structure, coat strength, and immune health. Proper zinc nutrition helps enrich normal hair growth and supports the body’s ability to renew skin and connective tissues.\xa0

Biotin plays a role in keratin production. Keratin is a primary\xa0component\xa0in structural protein found in hair, skin, and nails. Adequate biotin supports healthy hair growth and skin condition, contributing to stronger coats and healthy tissue renewal.\xa0

', 'Using Joint Supplements That Combine These Ingredients': 'No single ingredient can do everything to\xa0maintain\xa0exceptional mobility.\xa0That’s\xa0why a combination of glucosamine, chondroitin, O3FA, and green-lipped mussels work well together. They help\xa0maintain\xa0joint structure and cushioning, and support mobility.\xa0

When combined with these ingredients, MSM also helps reinforce the foundation of joint tissue while supporting everyday comfort and mobility as dogs age. This combination helps address multiple parts of the joint health. Cartilage development, connective tissue maintenance, moisture balance, and fluid movement are all better supported with these joint supplements.\xa0

', 'Signs Your Dog May Need Extra Support': 'The first sign that a dog may need support is through the quality and shine of their coat. Usually this\xa0presents as\xa0a “dull” coat, which means lacking in rich color. Their coats can also be rough, with brittle hair. All of these are indicators that greater nutritional support might be needed.\xa0\xa0\xa0

Increased shedding and excessive dander can also be signs of a\xa0poor quality\xa0coat.\xa0All of\xa0these issues may not be\xa0directly related\xa0to diet, but some nutritional intervention might be\xa0warranted. If you have concerns about your dog, talk to your veterinarian.\xa0\xa0\xa0

', 'Why Health Matters\xa0From\xa0the Inside Out': 'Good nutrition does more than support joints, skin, and mobility. It helps create\xa0the\xa0foundation for everything your dog does. title: What You Need to Know About Stem Cell Therapy for Dogs
author: Gemma Johnstone
intro:
The use of stem cells to promote healing is a growing area of interest in veterinary medicine. Stories of dramatic improvements in dogs with severe osteoarthritis or soft tissue injuries can make this regenerative therapy sound like a miracle cure. However, although early research is promising, particularly for certain orthopedic conditions, important questions remain about appropriate applications and long-term outcomes.

In This Article

If you’re considering this treatment option for your pet, here’s what you should know about the science, potential benefits, and current limitations of stem cell therapy for dogs.
full_content:
{'What Are Stem Cells?': 'Stem cells are unique, self-renewing cells that, under certain conditions, can change into other types of cells in a process called differentiation. No other cells have this natural flexibility, and stem cells play an important role in maintaining and repairing body tissue.

Stem cells may be totipotent (able to form all cell types, including embryonic tissues), pluripotent (able to form nearly all cell types), or multipotent (able to form multiple related cell types). In veterinary medicine, the current focus is on using adult mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), which are multipotent.

AKC is a participant in affiliate advertising programs designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees by advertising and linking to akc.org. If you purchase a product through this article, we may receive a portion of the sale.

', 'What Is Stem Cell Therapy for Dogs?': 'Mesenchymal stem cells are typically harvested from adipose (fat) tissue or bone marrow in dogs. They’re then administered through targeted treatment into parts of the musculoskeletal system, such as bones, cartilage, muscle, ligaments, or tendons.

“It’s important for pet owners to understand that stem cells are thought to help primarily by reducing inflammation within the joint and modifying the immune response, rather than regenerating new cartilage,” Christina Montalbano, VMD, DACVSMR (Canine), CCRP, CVA, CVMMP, CSCC, explains. Montalbano is a Clinical Assistant Professor of Integrative and Mobility Medicine in the department of Comparative, Diagnostic, and Population Medicine, at the College of Veterinary Medicine, University of Florida.

', 'How Effective Is Stem Cell Therapy for Dogs?': 'The science and research around stem cell treatment for dogs is evolving. Currently, the most common and studied use is intra-articular (joint) injection for canine osteoarthritis. It’s also used for tendon and ligament soft tissue injuries and, less commonly, certain nerve conditions.

AKC is a participant in affiliate advertising programs designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees by advertising and linking to akc.org. If you purchase a product through this article, we may receive a portion of the sale.

Some sources suggest potential benefits for kidney disease, liver disease, cardiomyopathy, or inflammatory skin and gastrointestinal conditions. However, evidence supporting these uses remains limited and often comes from small or preliminary studies.

Christopher W. Frye, DVM, DACVSMR (Canine), Associate Professor and Section Chief of Sports Medicine & Rehabilitation at Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine, is leading the only FDA-approved stem cell trial for canine and equine musculoskeletal and nervous conditions. He confirms that directly regrowing tissue from injected stem cells is unlikely with current technology. However, he says that there is definite potential to reduce inflammation and pain or support healing in some musculoskeletal conditions.

', 'Stem Cell Therapy Limitations': 'Dr. Frye points out that while the current data and research is promising, it has limitations. “The reality is that we know very little about the applications of stem cells in veterinary medicine and how best to use them,” he explains. Many studies have small sample sizes, lack control groups, or rely on subjective assessments. Key variables, such as dosing, timing, disease stage, and product type, remain unclear. Also, how dogs respond often depends on disease severity and other individual patient factors.

For these reasons, dog stem cell therapy is generally considered only as one component of a broader management plan rather than a replacement for established treatments such as weight management, rehabilitation, pain medications, and other orthobiologic therapies, such as platelet-rich plasma (PRP).

AKC is a participant in affiliate advertising programs designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees by advertising and linking to akc.org. If you purchase a product through this article, we may receive a portion of the sale.

Encouragingly, Dr. Frye acknowledges that as the research evolves, more targeted therapies are likely to be derived, and he is excited to see what the future holds.

', 'How Do Vets Administer Stem Cell Therapy?': 'In most cases, veterinarians administer stem cell therapy using a dog’s own cells (autologous therapy), and this involves three main stages.

AKC is a participant in affiliate advertising programs designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees by advertising and linking to akc.org. If you purchase a product through this article, we may receive a portion of the sale.

A veterinarian harvests a small amount of fat tissue under anesthesia, typically from your dog’s abdomen or shoulder.

Bone marrow stem cell collection may be performed relatively quickly under reversible sedation. It’s less invasive than intra-abdominal fat harvesting and requires less intensive lab processing. However, it’s a skilled procedure that requires additional training for most veterinarians.

For autologous stem cells, your dog’s collected tissue is sent to a laboratory, where the stem cells are isolated and expanded (grown). Processing typically takes 2-3 weeks to create a product for canine administration. Stem cells can be cryopreserved for many years in a viable state for future uses without additional harvesting procedures.

Your dog’s processed cells are often injected directly into the affected area. “Stem cells can be administered intra-articular [joints] for osteoarthritis, intra-muscular for muscle injuries, or intra-lesional for a tendon or ligament injury,” Dr. Montalbano says. Indirect applications have also been studied and applied, including intravenous applications.

Dr. Montalbano explains that clinicians sometimes co-inject stem cells for osteoarthritis with other biologic products, such as platelet-rich plasma or hyaluronic acid. Both of these improve treatment efficacy compared with using any of these products alone. However, researchers cannot make strong conclusions regarding therapeutic combinations due to limited published research.

Most direct injections are performed on an outpatient basis while your dog is under sedation. This helps to ensure accurate needle placement and comfort. Vets can perform intravenous (IV) applications on an appropriately-monitored, awake patient.

According to Dr. Montalbano, after care instructions for most direct applications typically involve monitoring the injection site for heat, swelling, or an increase in pain or lameness.

AKC is a participant in affiliate advertising programs designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees by advertising and linking to akc.org. If you purchase a product through this article, we may receive a portion of the sale.

Activity restriction is often recommended for at least 1-2 weeks following joint injections to allow any transient inflammation or pain sometimes seen related to the injection to subside.

When dealing with soft tissue injuries, your dog will typically be on a structured rehabilitation plan. You should follow this plan carefully to promote the best all-around results.



', 'What Are the Risks and Side Effects?': 'In the short term, mesenchymal stem cell therapy appears\xa0relatively safe\xa0in current published studies. However, you should weigh up the inherent risks associated with tissue collection (including sedation or anesthesia) and administration, particularly in older dogs or those with underlying health conditions.\xa0

AKC is a participant in affiliate advertising programs designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees by advertising and linking to akc.org. If you purchase a product through this article, we may receive a portion of the sale.

According to Dr. Montalbano, intra-articular injections have been reported to sometimes cause a temporary joint flare. “This refers to an increase in post-injection joint pain beyond that typically expected from the procedure itself and thought to be reactionary to the injectate; although it is still transient and\xa0typically is\xa0self-limiting in\xa03-7\xa0days,” she says.\xa0

Infection, cartilage injury, or injection-site complications related to the procedure itself are rare but also possible.\xa0

Data\xa0regarding\xa0safety and effectiveness of these products and their applications is being collected with a particular need for longer term follow up. As Dr. Frye points out, stem cell therapy is currently considered an experimental or new animal drug by the\xa0FDA;\xa0clinical field studies are ongoing, and misinformation exists around the internet.\xa0

“As with any biologic product, quality control, processing methods, and regulatory oversight may vary between manufacturers, so owners should seek treatment from veterinarians experienced in regenerative medicine,” Dr. Montalbano advises.\xa0

', 'When Is It Worth Considering Stem Cell Therapy for Your Dog?': 'Stem cell therapy for dogs can be\xa0costly and\xa0is still considered\xa0experimental.\xa0For this reason, Dr. Montalbano recommends owners discuss expected benefits, risks, and alternatives with their veterinarian before pursuing this treatment for musculoskeletal conditions.\xa0

The cost of stem cell therapy for dogs can vary widely depending on the individual clinic and the condition being treated. However, it typically costs between $3,000 and $5,000. This includes fees for the\xa0initial\xa0consultation, cell harvesting, processing, and injections.\xa0

Be aware that traditional pet insurance plans may not cover this experimental type of treatment.\xa0

AKC is a participant in affiliate advertising programs designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees by advertising and linking to akc.org. If you purchase a product through this article, we may receive a portion of the sale.

Another consideration is that stem cell therapy treatment for dogs is only available at specialized orthopedic centers or veterinary hospitals. Most general veterinary practices\xa0don’t\xa0have the equipment, clinical environment, or\xa0expertise\xa0to process stem cells. This could create logistical challenges if there\xa0isn’t\xa0a center near you.\xa0

Stem cell therapy may be\xa0considered as\xa0an option\xa0in some patients within a broader management plan rather than a replacement for conventional therapies. “Weight management, controlled exercise, and rehabilitation are critical components of long-term success,” Dr. Montalbano says.\xa0

Although some studies show stem cells may improve comfort and mobility for some patients,\xa0it’s\xa0important to remember that stem cell therapy is not a cure for canine osteoarthritis or soft tissue injuries. Instead, it should be viewed as a promising but developing tool that requires realistic expectations and careful veterinary guidance.\xa0

title: Aspiration Pneumonia in Dogs: Causes, Signs, and Treatment
author: Gemma Johnstone
intro:
If your dog accidentally inhales food, water, vomit or other foreign materials into their lungs, it can cause aspiration pneumonia. Left to progress, this serious lung infection can become life-threatening.

In This Article

Being aware of the risk factors and early signs of aspiration pneumonia in dogs means you can take prompt action. With timely veterinary diagnosis and treatment, many dogs make a full recovery.
full_content:
{'What Is Aspiration Pneumonia in Dogs?': '“Aspiration pneumonia occurs when the contents of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, which includes the mouth, end up in the respiratory tract and ultimately the lungs,” Dr. Adesola Odunayo, DVM, a Michael Schaer Endowed Distinguished Professor of Emergency and Critical Care Medicine at the University of Florida, explains.

To better understand the mechanics, think of a time when you’ve taken a drink and ended up coughing aggressively because something “went down the wrong way.” This sensation occurs when the liquid goes down your trachea (windpipe) and into your lungs rather than down your food pipe (esophagus) into your stomach.

Dogs can also experience this, and if they don’t cough up the offending material, aspiration pneumonia can be a complication of pulmonary aspiration (the accidental inhalation of something other than air into the lungs).

If food, water, saliva, stomach acid, vomit, or a small foreign object ends up in your dog’s lungs, this causes inflammation of the airway, and bacteria can grow, leading to a rapidly progressing infection.

', 'What Causes Aspiration Pneumonia in Dogs?': 'Dr. Odunayo says vomiting and regurgitation are the most common reasons aspiration pneumonia occurs in dogs. “Typically, during the act of vomiting, the body naturally protects the respiratory tract so that gastrointestinal contents stay out of the airways,” she explains. “In some instances, this doesn’t happen, and GI contents may accidentally get inhaled into the lungs.”

Certain factors and conditions, especially those that reduce the ability to protect the airways, can increase the risk of a dog developing aspiration pneumonia. These include:

', 'Signs of Aspiration Pneumonia in Dogs': '“Aspiration pneumonia most often causes general signs of unwellness and, depending on its severity, dogs may also have varying respiratory signs,” Dr. Odunayo says. While they can be wide-ranging and non-specific, some common signs include:

Dr. Odunayo says you may also see increased use of accessory muscles to assist with breathing (usually the abdominal muscles).

“In severe cases, you may also notice your dog breathing with their mouth open and/or a blue or purple discoloration of the gums and/or tongue,” she says. While it’s important to consult with a vet if your dog is experiencing any of the above signs, acute respiratory distress is a medical emergency, and you should contact your veterinary hospital immediately.

Even if your dog hasn’t vomited recently, be aware that signs of infection can develop days or weeks after pulmonary aspiration occurs.

', 'Diagnosing Aspiration Pneumonia in Dogs': 'Aspiration pneumonia can be challenging to diagnose definitively, and mild signs may be similar to symptoms your dog may experience with other conditions, such as kennel cough or even heart disease.

However, your veterinarian may suspect this condition after taking your dog’s history. For example, if they’re experiencing chronic vomiting, difficulty swallowing, or are recovering from surgery under anesthesia, this can offer vital clues.

Dr. Ashly Smith, Regional Medical Director for Small Door Veterinary, explains that veterinarians commonly diagnose aspiration pneumonia through a combination of physical examination, chest X-rays, and blood work to assess infection and inflammation. “In some cases, they may recommend airway sampling (such as a tracheal wash) to identify the specific bacteria involved and guide antibiotic selection,” she says.

Your veterinarian may also perform other tests to rule out other conditions or to diagnose possible underlying causes of the aspiration pneumonia.

', 'Treating Aspiration Pneumonia in Dogs': 'Treatment of aspiration pneumonia depends on its severity. “Dogs who are mildly affected are treated with oral antibiotics on an outpatient basis, with specific instructions for signs to watch out for that may indicate progressive disease,” Dr. Odunayo says.

Pets who are moderately to severely affected usually have difficulty achieving normal blood oxygen levels. “Those patients are hospitalized with supplemental oxygen therapy, intravenous antibiotics, and other supportive care as indicated,” Dr. Odunayo says. This may include IV fluids, and anti-nausea and GI motility medications.

Treatment duration varies depending on the severity of the aspiration pneumonia and any underlying causes. Be prepared for it to last anywhere from 10 days to two months.

When your veterinarian identifies an underlying and manageable cause for aspiration pneumonia, they will also treat this.

', 'Prognosis for Dogs with Aspiration Pneumonia': 'The good news is that with prompt diagnosis and treatment (before infection sets in too deeply), most dogs with aspiration pneumonia recover well. However, the severity of the disease influences the prognosis.

“Dogs who need more intensive care (high flow oxygen or mechanical ventilation) tend not to do as well as pets who are mildly affected and have little to no need for supplemental oxygen,” Dr. Odunayo says. “Pets with underlying causes that are more challenging to manage (e.g. laryngeal paralysis, megaesophagus) also don’t do as well due to the increased risk for recurrent aspiration.”

For dogs that make a full recovery, expect it to take anything from a week to more than a month for them to feel fully like themselves again. Your veterinarian may also carry out follow-up imaging to help confirm that the lungs are healing well.

', 'Preventing Aspiration Pneumonia in Dogs': 'It’s not possible to prevent aspiration pneumonia in all cases. However, you can reduce the chances of it developing if you identify situations where your dog could be at risk.
Dr. Smith recommends addressing conditions that affect swallowing or reflux, avoiding force-feeding, and following any pre-anesthesia and post-anesthesia feeding and medication instructions. “For dogs with chronic regurgitation [i.e. those with megaesophagus] or neurologic issues, feeding smaller, upright meals and monitoring closely after eating can also help prevent aspiration,” she says.

title: Why Is My Dog Drinking So Much Water? Polydipsia or Excessive Thirst in Dogs
author: Gemma Johnstone
intro:
If you’re noticing your dog’s water bowl needs filling up more often and they’re asking to go out more frequently, this isn’t something to ignore. While it’s normal to feel more thirsty when the weather is hot or after doing some exercise, a dog regularly drinking a lot of water can be one of the earliest clues that they have an underlying health problem.

In This Article

Taking prompt action when you spot excessive thirst (polydipsia) in your dog gives them the best chance of making a good recovery. There are many possible causes of polydipsia, and your veterinarian will need to take a systematic approach to identify the cause and start appropriate treatment.
full_content:
{'What Is Polydipsia in Dogs?': 'Polydipsia in dogs is defined as excessive thirst and/or excessive drinking. Because what goes in must come out, dogs with polydipsia usually experience polyuria, which is an increase in urination. You may see this referred to as PU/PD in veterinary notes.

Deborah Mandell, VMD, is a Professor and Director of Emergency Services at Matthew J. Ryan Veterinary Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania. She explains that an underlying medical condition often causes increased urination, leading the dog to drink more to compensate for the loss.

“If a pet doesn’t increase the amount of water they take in, they can actually become dehydrated or worse, due to the increased amount of water lost in the urine,” Dr. Mandell says. “This dehydration and decreased volume of water in the body trigger the brain to increase thirst and thus increase drinking.”

', 'What’s Considered Normal Water Intake for Dogs?': 'Dogs drink around 40 to 60 milliliters of water per kilogram of body weight daily . However, water intake naturally fluctuates day to day for each dog and varies depending on factors such as weather, activity level, and diet.

When your dog is thirsty after a hike on a warm day, it’s not typically a medical concern. What matters most is the pattern. If you notice your dog drinking more than usual, it may be an indicator of something more serious.

“Technically, polydipsia is generally considered when a dog drinks more than 100ml/kg of body weight daily,” Brian Collins, DVM with the Cornell Riney Canine Health Center at the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine, says. However, even smaller daily amounts can be a sign of an underlying problem if they represent a significant change from your dog’s normal baseline.

Keeping a note of your dog’s drinking habits can help you spot anything out of the ordinary. Signs of excessive thirst or drinking may include needing to refill your dog’s water bowl more often, an increase in how many bathroom breaks they need, and any changes in their appetite or energy levels.

', 'Common Causes of Polydipsia in Dogs': 'Dogs drinking excessively is common, in part because there are over 30 underlying medical causes for polyuria and polydipsia.

“Certain conditions result in primary polydipsia (where they first cause increased drinking),” Dr. Collins explains. “However, in the majority of cases, the condition causes primary polyuria (increased loss of urine) and then compensatory polydipsia follows.”

The most common causes of polydipsia are diabetes mellitus, Cushing’s disease, and chronic kidney disease. All of these start out with polyuria.

“Another relatively common condition is hypercalcemia (elevated calcium levels in the blood), which actually occurs secondary to numerous conditions, including kidney disease, various types of cancer, and fungal diseases,” Dr. Collins says. “Other relatively common causes of polydipsia include pyometra (infection of the uterus), liver disease, and medications that can cause increased drinking.”

While not as common, E. coli or Leptospirosis bacterial infections of the kidney are also noteworthy causes of polydipsia.

In rare cases, behavioral factors can cause a dog to drink excessively. Known as psychogenic polydipsia, this primary form is typically seen in young, hyperactive, anxious, or stressed dogs. It results in the dog binging on water, even when their body doesn’t physically require rehydration.

', 'Signs of Polydipsia in Dogs': 'While it isn’t normally practical or necessary to measure the exact amount of water your dog drinks daily, being observant of general changes can help alert you to polydipsia. Some things to look out for include:

“Other clinical signs will depend on the underlying cause [of polydipsia] and may include lethargy, weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, panting, and either increased or decreased appetite,” Dr. Collins says.

', 'How the Vet Diagnoses Polydipsia': 'Identifying why your dog is drinking excessively is key to successful treatment and improving the outlook. However, because polydipsia can be a symptom of one of many possible underlying causes, this can make diagnosis challenging.

Diagnosis begins with your veterinarian noting your observations and collecting a thorough history. They will likely ask how long the increase has been occurring, roughly how much water your dog consumes daily, whether multiple pets share a bowl, and whether the frequency and duration of urination have changed.

According to Dr. Collins, initial laboratory testing to screen for causes of polydipsia typically includes a complete blood count (CBC), a chemistry panel, and a urinalysis. Then, other more advanced testing may be required based on the results of the initial tests.

Dr. Mandell warns that you should never do a water deprivation test at home without talking to your veterinarian. You might read online about how this test can evaluate your dog’s ability to concentrate urine , which can be helpful for diagnosing Diabetes Insipidus. However, she explains that it can have serious life-threatening complications, and there are other safer alternative diagnostic tools.

', 'Treating Polydipsia in Dogs': 'For more common secondary polydipsia, the focus is on treating the underlying cause. Below is an outline of possible treatment approaches for common conditions that can lead to excessive thirst and urination.

Never restrict your dog’s water intake unless under your veterinarian’s guidance. Doing so can cause dangerous dehydration and electrolyte imbalances.

', 'Outlook for Dogs With Polydipsia': 'Your dog’s outlook depends on the underlying cause of the polydipsia and its progression. Some issues, like urinary tract infections, can be easy to treat. Others, like diabetes or Cushing’s disease, may require lifelong management, but your dog can still live a good quality of life if the condition is well-controlled.

title: Hyperkeratosis in Dogs: Signs, Symptoms, Treatments
author: Colt Dodd
intro:
Hyperkeratosis refers to the overproduction of keratin, the protein that makes up a dog’s hair, skin, and nails. Depending on the cause, hyperkeratosis may manifest as ashy skin around the hinge joints, rough, hardened paw pads, or a dry nose. While hyperkeratosis commonly presents in older, more sedentary dogs, it may also result from an underlying health condition.

Key Points

“From a clinical standpoint, the question is rarely just ‘Is this hyperkeratosis?’ The real question is, ‘Is this normal for this dog, or is it a sign of something else?’ That is where veterinary evaluation becomes important,” says Dr. Jo Myers, DVM at Vetster in Salida, Colorado.

Understanding how to identify hyperkeratosis and when to consult a veterinarian can help you prioritize your dog’s health, safety, and comfort.
full_content:
{'What Is Canine Hyperkeratosis?': 'Dr. Myers clears up a common misunderstanding about hyperkeratosis. She shares that hyperkeratosis isn’t a diagnosis itself, but a clue about a dog’s health profile. Essentially, hyperkeratosis tells the veterinarian what the skin looks like – not why.

AKC is a participant in affiliate advertising programs designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees by advertising and linking to akc.org. If you purchase a product through this article, we may receive a portion of the sale.

“If you break the word apart, ‘hyper’ means excessive, ‘kerato’ refers to keratin, the structural protein that makes up skin, hair, and nails, and ‘osis’ indicates a condition. So, hyperkeratosis literally means excessive keratin production in the outer layer of the skin,” says Dr. Myers. “In dogs, we most often notice it on the paw pads or the nose. It can look like thickened, rough, crusty, scaly, or even ‘hairy’ projections of hardened skin.”

Often, hyperkeratosis is skin-deep and not a veterinary emergency. Monitoring the affected area can help you stay on top of any changes to your dog’s health and act if a problem arises.

“In many dogs, especially seniors, mild thickening is more of a cosmetic issue than a medical emergency. The goal is not to make the skin perfectly smooth. The goal is to keep it comfortable, intact, and free of infection,” says Dr. Myers.

', 'Potential Causes of Canine Hyperkeratosis': 'Hyperkeratosis can result from a host of different factors, some of which include:

“Most of the time when I see hyperkeratosis in everyday practice, it’s either mild age-related thickening, a breed- or lifestyle-related normal variation, or secondary to some other chronic skin disease,” says Dr. Myers.

', 'Treatments for Hyperkeratosis': 'There isn’t a one-size-fits-all remedy for hyperkeratosis because many scenarios and conditions can cause it.

AKC is a participant in affiliate advertising programs designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees by advertising and linking to akc.org. If you purchase a product through this article, we may receive a portion of the sale.

“Treatment depends entirely on what is causing the hyperkeratosis. Because hyperkeratosis is a physical finding, not a diagnosis, the first step is determining which category it falls into,” says Dr. Myers. “If hyperkeratosis is secondary to an underlying disease, treatment focuses on that primary condition … If hyperkeratosis is mild and age-related, or related to chronic pressure, management may be very simple and conservative.”

Treating diseases that cause hyperkeratosis may involve antibiotics, intravenous fluids, or various lifestyle changes. Managing hyperkeratosis in an older dog may call for applying veterinary paw balms, monitoring the affected areas, and observing for other signs of illness. A veterinarian may also recommend periodic trimming if the keratin overgrowths are severe.

“It is important not to aggressively peel or cut thickened tissue at home. Over-trimming can cause pain, bleeding, and infection,” advises Dr. Myers.

', 'What Dogs Are Most Likely to Experience Hyperkeratosis?': "This can be a tricky question because hyperkeratosis isn’t a medical condition itself but an indicator of something else. To put matters in context, Dr. Myers compares the question of, “Are certain breeds predisposed to hyperkeratosis?” to “Are certain breeds predisposed to coughing?”

But whether because of their anatomy or predisposition to illnesses that cause hyperkeratosis, some breeds that are susceptible to the condition include:

“From a pet owner’s perspective, the more helpful question is usually not, ‘Is my dog’s breed predisposed to hyperkeratosis?’ It is, ‘Is what I’m seeing normal for my dog?'” says Dr. Myers. “Owning a northern breed does not mean you should be on high alert for hyperkeratosis. Most Huskies, Malamutes, and other breeds with thicker pads or drier noses are completely healthy. What matters more than breed is change and comfort.”

", 'Can Hyperkeratosis Cause Joint Pain?': 'You may see a senior dog with hyperkeratosis, note their stiff walking pattern, and attribute the skin condition to their joints. After all, hyperkeratosis is more likely to form on thin parts of the body, such as along the hinge joints, as a dog ages. However, the two are unrelated.
